```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment="#>")
library(spseg)
library(dplyr)
```

`spseg()` can measure several attributes in one call. It discovers neighbors
once per focal location for all requested variables and bands; adaptive kNN
discovery can internally expand its candidate query. It remains single-threaded.
The caller can parallelize independent cities or simulation runs.

# Inputs and syntax

Each row represents a geographic support point or an aggregated population.
An `sf` object uses its active geometry column, with polygon centroids as
support points. A plain data frame supplies `coords = c("x", "y")`.
Distances are Euclidean in coordinate units; project geographic coordinates
appropriately before requesting bandwidths in meters.

```{r individuals}
people <- data.frame(
  x = 1:12, y = rep(0, 12),
  ethnicity = rep(c("a", "b", "c"), 4),
  education = ordered(rep(c("primary", "secondary", "tertiary"), each=4),
                      levels=c("primary", "secondary", "tertiary")),
  income = c(0, 0, 10, 10, 20, 30, 40, 40, 50, 60, 80, 100),
  age = c(18, 20, 20, 25, 30, 31, 35, 40, 45, 50, 60, 70)
)
variables <- list(
  ethnicity = spseg_categorical(vars="ethnicity"),
  education = spseg_ordinal(vars="education"),
  income = spseg_continuous(vars="income"),
  age = spseg_continuous(vars="age")
)
result <- spseg(people, coords=c("x", "y"), variables=variables,
                measures="all", bands=c(2, 4), scope="overall")
as.data.frame(result)
```

`spseg_ordinal(vars=...)` requires an ordered factor or explicit `levels`.
`spseg_continuous(vars=..., representation="intervals", levels=...)` describes
membership in intervals of an underlying continuous variable. The default
`representation="exact"` instead requires numeric observations. Supplied
interval labels do not determine numerical spacing. A single column in `vars`
selects observed memberships or values; multiple columns select counts. For
long-form aggregated data, select the membership/value column and supply the
population-count column as `weights`, with locations repeated across categories.
These and `spseg_categorical()` are the three specification
constructors; interval input uses the same continuous constructor as exact input.

```{r aggregates}
blocks <- data.frame(x=1:4, y=0,
                     low=c(8, 4, 2, 1), middle=c(1, 3, 5, 2), high=c(1, 3, 3, 7))
aggregate_result <- spseg(
  blocks, coords=c("x", "y"),
  variables=list(
    education=spseg_ordinal(vars=c("low", "middle", "high")),
    income=spseg_continuous(vars=c("low", "middle", "high"),
                            representation="intervals"),
    exact_age=spseg_continuous(vars=c("low", "middle", "high"), scores=c(20, 40, 60))
  ), bands=c(0, 2), measures=c("information", "diversity", "square_root", "dissimilarity")
)
as.data.frame(aggregate_result)
```

The three specifications in this example make different claims about the
*same count table*: ordered categories, unobserved continuous intervals, or
exact values. A single area mean does not recover its residents' distribution.
Exact-value count input is never expanded into individual records.
Interval input uses linear CDF interpolation in global percentile space and
does not impute individual incomes or use bin midpoints. In the new continuous
summary interface, categories are proportionally apportioned across the requested
global groups when needed, preserving the requested probability grid. The same
fractions apply to original focal counts and local target shares at every location.
This assumes a common within-category rank distribution across locations, without
requiring monetary lower/upper tail bounds. A brief warning flags interpolation;
neighborhood diagnostics and global allocation fractions are retained. `scores`
and absolute summary `cuts`
apply only to exact input; `levels` and `interpolation` apply only to interval
input.

Each specification can override `measures`. The common selectors are
`"information"`, `"diversity"`, `"dissimilarity"`, `"square_root"`, and `"exposure"`.
`"relative_diversity"` and `"variance_ratio"` are aliases for the diversity
family; the nominal measure is specifically relative diversity, not the other
multigroup indices that share its binary reduction. `"all"` includes all five families.
`scope = "overall"` selects categorical multigroup indices, ordinal
cumulative-threshold indices, or continuous rank-order indices.
`scope = "pairwise"` selects comparisons between categorical/ordinal categories
or resolved continuous groups; `"both"` is the default. Exposure is selected
separately through `measures`.

## Variable-specific output

Each variable can override `scope`, `output`, `keep_scores`, and
`keep_contributions`, as well as `measures`. `NULL` in a variable specification
inherits the corresponding global setting. An explicit `FALSE` overrides a
global retention setting of `TRUE`.

```{r variable-output}
mixed_output <- spseg(
  blocks, coords = c("x", "y"), bands = c(2, 4),
  variables = list(
    groups = spseg_categorical(vars = c("low", "middle", "high"),
      scope = "both", output = "full"),
    education = spseg_ordinal(vars = c("low", "middle", "high"),
      keep_contributions = TRUE)
  ),
  scope = "overall", output = "indices"
)
mixed_output$analyses$groups$settings
mixed_output$analyses$education$settings
head(as.data.frame(mixed_output, what = "env"))
```

Extraction across all variables includes the analyses with the requested stored
results. In this example, the environment table contains only `groups`.
Selecting `variables = "education"` explicitly when requesting environments
reports that they were not retained. Shared spatial inputs are stored once.

# Population and spatial contributions

Let $m_{iv}$ be the eligible population for variable $v$ at support point $i$.
Index averaging weights are $\alpha_{iv}=m_{iv}/\sum_i m_{iv}$.
Counts supply this mass through their row totals. Observed values use a
specification's `weights`, otherwise the common `population`, otherwise one
per row. Missing values fail by default. `na.action="omit"` sets only that
variable's eligible mass to zero for affected rows (entire count rows if any
category is missing). Missing population weights are always invalid.

For kNN, each variable uses its own eligible population for neighbor selection.
An ethnicity neighborhood of 100 residents and an income neighborhood of 100
adults can therefore have different radii. `population` supplies default
weights for observed values; descriptor `weights` override it, and count
specifications always use their own row totals. With no supplied weights,
kNN observed-value rows each represent one person. For radius neighborhoods,
the reference `population` also controls population-based default distance
bands. It can be inferred when count or weight totals agree; supply it when
those totals differ. Multiple marginal count tables need no joint
cross-tabulation for these separate analyses; they cannot identify joint
ethnicity-by-income outcomes.

```{r knn}
spseg(people, coords=c("x", "y"), variables=variables,
      neighbors="knn", bands=c(3, 6), measures="information")
```

Let $\lambda_{ijbv}$ combine the selected kernel and the population inclusion
fraction for band $b$ and variable $v$. Radius contributions are shared across
variables; kNN contributions are shared when eligible populations coincide.
Local category or value masses sum $\lambda_{ijbv}$ times the source mass, then
normalize to shares. This weights people, rather than averaging unit shares
without accounting for population.

kNN selects exactly the requested eligible population **before distance
weighting**, to numerical precision. It includes the focal support unit first,
fractionally if its population exceeds the threshold, then adds other units
by distance and includes the boundary distance group proportionately. Kernel weighting can
reduce the resulting effective population; normalized kernel distances use
each variable's selected radius. An error identifies any variable whose
total eligible population is below the requested threshold. The shared
candidate iterator advances until all variable populations can reach the largest
threshold; variables with identical populations also reuse contributions.


Each analysis's `knn` table records the requested population and the minimum
and maximum selected population and radius across eligible focal rows. For
example, `result$analyses$income$knn` audits the income neighborhoods after a
kNN call. Categorical `scope="pairwise"` compares groups within the variable's
selected neighborhoods; it does not select a new neighborhood for every pair.
To select 100 members of a particular pair, supply a separate categorical
specification with only those two count columns.

The focal unit enters first. All other units at the boundary distance receive
the same population inclusion fraction, making boundary selection independent
of row order. This geographic convention is separate from ties in the attribute.
Radius zero includes all coincident support points, matching the existing
radius-search implementation; with distinct support points it uses the focal
unit's distribution. Individual-level radius zero need not describe a
substantively useful neighborhood.

# Measure definitions and provenance

The mathematical definitions now have a dedicated technical guide:
`vignette("spseg-measure-definitions")`. It gives the local variation and
deviation functions, regional normalizers, multigroup and pairwise formulas,
and their relationship to Reardon and colleagues' work. It distinguishes
published definitions from package supplements, empirical rank conventions,
and interval-interpolation assumptions.

The guide also explains which expressions require nonoverlapping units,
how local scores differ from additive index contributions, and why compact
plotting summaries do not necessarily support exact index reconstruction.
This vignette concentrates on specifying variables and interpreting outputs.

# Exposure and isolation

For categorical variables, exposure is **unnormalized**: it averages local
target-group shares over members of a focal group. Diagonals describe
isolation; off-diagonals describe exposure to other groups. See the technical
guide for the formula and its distinction from normalized scalar exposure.

Continuous variables use one summary specification. Shares are the default;
the default interior probabilities `.25`, `.5`, and `.75` define four global
focal/target income groups. Exact tied values stay together, so achieved group
sizes need not be equal. For interval input, the requested grid is preserved.
If the highest category contains 15% of the regional population, a top-decile
group receives `10/15` of that category's population in every unit. This is an
explicit model-based allocation, not observed membership within that category.
The allocation is fixed before surface construction and used for both focal and
neighbor populations. A warning flags interpolation, while extraction with
`what = "interpolation"` reports `bottom_category_share`, `top_category_share`, and
`interpolated_share`, by location and band. The latter is the weighted local share
in categories split across groups, not a statistical error estimate. Allocation
fractions are in `definition$summary$groups$allocation`. Choosing probabilities
on supplied interval cumulative boundaries avoids interpolation of membership.

```{r exposure}
income_units <- data.frame(
  unit = c("U", "V"),
  x = c(0, 1),
  y = 0,
  income_10 = c(2, 0),
  income_20 = c(1, 1),
  income_30 = c(0, 2),
  income_40 = c(1, 1)
)
income_columns <- paste0("income_", c(10, 20, 30, 40))

share_result <- spseg(
  income_units,
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  variables = list(income = spseg_continuous(
    vars = income_columns,
    scores = c(10, 20, 30, 40),
    summary = list(type = "shares", probs = 0.5)
  )),
  bands = 0,
  weighting = "unweighted",
  measures = "all",
  scope = "both",
  output = "full"
)

as.data.frame(share_result, what = "exposure") |>
  filter(band == 0) |>
  select(from_group, to_group, value)
```

There are eight people, two in each income category. Their global weighted
midranks are `1/8`, `3/8`, `5/8`, and `7/8`. The median cut at income 20 gives
the local low/high shares `(3/4, 1/4)` at U and `(1/4, 3/4)` at V. Low-income
focal people weight U and V by `(3/4, 1/4)`; high-income focal people weight
them by `(1/4, 3/4)`. The resulting exposure rows are low `(5/8, 3/8)` and
high `(3/8, 5/8)`. These are average local shares, not shares from pooling all
neighbor counts first.

With `type = "quantiles"`, the same `probs` vector defines global focal groups
and within-neighborhood quantile positions. The grouped result is the
focal-population-weighted average of each person's local rank quantile; it is
not the quantile of a pooled neighborhood distribution. `mean_rank = TRUE`
adds a distinct mean of the full local rank distribution, not a mean of the
reported quantiles.

```{r rank-summaries}
rank_result <- spseg(
  income_units,
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  variables = list(income = spseg_continuous(
    vars = income_columns,
    scores = c(10, 20, 30, 40),
    summary = list(type = "quantiles", probs = 0.5, mean_rank = TRUE)
  )),
  bands = 0,
  weighting = "unweighted",
  measures = "exposure",
  output = "full"
)

rank_profiles <- as.data.frame(rank_result, what = "exposure")
rank_profiles |>
  filter(band == 0) |>
  select(from_group, statistic, prob, value)
```

At U and V the local mean ranks are `3/8` and `5/8`; local median ranks are
`1/8` and `5/8`. Averaging by focal income gives low/high mean ranks `7/16`
and `9/16`, and low/high median ranks `1/4` and `1/2`. `what = "exposure"`
keeps the familiar request: share tables contain `from_group`, `to_group`, and
`value`, while quantile tables contain `from_group`, `statistic`, `prob`, and
`value`. Mean-rank rows use
`statistic = "mean_rank"` and a missing `prob`. Rank profiles are descriptive,
not classic exposure matrices or segregation indices.

Use `scope = "pairwise"` (or `"both"`) for binary indices between the resolved
continuous groups. These comparisons renormalize local shares within each
selected pair and use neighborhoods selected from the full eligible income
population. With the two median-defined groups above, the binary dissimilarity
is `.5`. Pairwise indices are separate from both the continuous scalar indices
and the directional exposure matrix.

For exact income, `cuts` can replace `probs` in shares mode, for example
`summary = list(type = "shares", cuts = c(30, 60))`; the cut groups include
implicit open-ended tails. Absolute cuts are not accepted for interval input,
whose labels do not establish monetary thresholds. Continuous variables use
`summary`, not the removed `localenv` and `exposure` arguments. Summary settings leave
the full-resolution continuous scalar indices and their normalizers unchanged.

# Results and properties

`result$analyses[[name]]` contains scalar and optional pairwise indices,
exposure summaries, method metadata, actual normalizers, and per-band status.
`as.data.frame()` returns compact identifiers and a single `value` column.
Type, method, and representation remain in `analyses[[name]]$definition`;
`what = "diagnostics"` extracts per-band status and kNN diagnostics.
`output="full"` or `"localenv"` retains compact local summaries. Categorical
and ordinal variables default to category shares. Continuous variables use one
`summary` setting for local output and focal-group summaries. The default
shares mode groups exact values at global quartiles; interval input preserves
the requested grid by proportionally allocating categories that cross group
boundaries in global-percentile space. Explicit
`summary = list(type = "quantiles")` returns local quantiles of **global
population ranks**, not original income units, and their focal-group averages.
A local median rank of `.8` locates the weighted median neighbor at the
population's 80th percentile. Kernel weights, population weights, and kNN
boundary fractions enter local summaries.

For ordinal categories and exact observations, ties have global weighted
midranks and local quantiles select the first rank at which cumulative local
weight reaches the requested probability. They do not interpolate between
observed ranks. For grouped intervals, local quantile values invert the
piecewise-linear local CDF in global percentile space, using the requested
probability grid. Fractional category allocation assumes a common
within-category rank distribution across locations. The implicit global
endpoints do not add local minimum or maximum rows. An empty local environment
has missing summaries.

Continuous summary choices do not change the full-resolution scalar indices.
The former continuous `localenv`/`exposure` arguments have been removed.
Ordinal summaries retain their existing `localenv` control. For example,
request local rank quantiles for exact income and education together:

```{r compact-environments}
environments <- spseg(people, coords=c("x", "y"), bands=3, output="full",
  variables=list(
    income=spseg_continuous(vars="income",
      summary=list(type="quantiles", probs=c(.25, .5, .75), mean_rank=TRUE)),
    education=spseg_ordinal(vars="education", localenv="quantiles")
  ))
head(as.data.frame(environments, what="env", variables="income"))
as.data.frame(environments, what="exposure", variables="income")
```

Use `as.data.frame(result, what="env")` or `sf::st_as_sf(result)` to obtain
long local tables. Quantile tables have `statistic`, `prob`, and `value`;
category-share tables have `category` and `value`. Grouped tables from
`what="exposure"` use `from_group`, `to_group`, and `value` for share
probabilities; rank profiles use `from_group`, `statistic`, `prob`, and `value`.
Columns follow the selected summary types; mixed tables contain their union,
with `statistic="share"` identifying share rows. Mean-rank rows use `statistic="mean_rank"`
and have no quantile probability. `definition$summary` records the requested
and effective global grid, resolved groups, interval allocation, and interpolation
reasons. Detailed local distributions are used transiently and not retained.

An exact constant variable has undefined scalar indices (`NA`, status
`"constant"`), but its exposure can be one. A single populated *interval*
still represents unobserved within-interval variation under interpolation;
its rank-order indices are zero rather than an observed-constant assertion.
Positive-mass focal units with no eligible local population give
`"empty_environment"` and undefined band results. Empty focal exposure groups
have undefined rows. Values are not clamped: for overlapping spatial
environments, the population-weighted mixture of local CDFs need not equal
the regional CDF. Variation ratios can be negative, and bounds/proofs based
on nonoverlapping partitions must not be assumed for every spatial analogue.

There is no fixed-geometry cache, grouping argument, or internal parallelism.

# Population surfaces and development status

For polygonal `sf` data, `surface="grid"` and `surface="pycno"` accept count
specifications for all requested variables. All count columns are transported
through one grid construction, then each variable is calculated using its own
count table and eligible population. Exact continuous count inputs retain their
`scores`. Observed-value specifications use raw support; an area mean does not
supply a resident-level distribution to interpolate.

```{r multi-surface}
polygons <- sf::st_make_grid(sf::st_as_sfc(sf::st_bbox(
  c(xmin=0,ymin=0,xmax=2,ymax=2))), n=c(2,2))
areas <- sf::st_sf(blocks, geometry=polygons)
gridded <- spseg(areas,
  variables=list(education=spseg_ordinal(vars=c("low","middle","high")),
                 income=spseg_continuous(representation = "intervals", vars=c("low","middle","high"))),
  surface="grid", nrow=4, ncol=4, bands=1, output="full")
as.data.frame(gridded)
```

The package is in pre-1.0 development. Use a named `variables` list for
explicit specifications, or column-name shorthand for one categorical
analysis. Results use `result$analyses[[variable_name]]`; stored environments
contain the requested share or rank summaries. There is no compatibility
calling convention for the original seg API. Mathematical definitions and
sources are collected in `vignette("spseg-measure-definitions")`.
